c.tagline: Costa Blanca sun, a hilltop castle, and a palm-lined esplanade.

taxi.fareNote: White taxis show a green light when free; fares are metered with fixed airport supplements. Book via app (Uber, Bolt, FreeNow, Cabify) or a radio-taxi line.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

hood_landmark.Benalúa: Casa Mediterráneo, in the old Benalúa railway station

avoid.reason: Watch for pickpockets along the Explanada de España, on the beaches, and in the El Barrio nightlife lanes late at night.

hood_desc: The old town climbing the castle hill in tangled lanes of whitewashed, flower-draped houses below Santa Bárbara Castle; the historic heart, and the core of Alicante's nightlife known locally as 'El Barrio'.
The elegant 19th-century grid of wide boulevards around the Rambla de Méndez Núñez and Mercado Central, with El Corte Inglés and smart shops; a convenient, central base.
The seafront strip beside the marble-wave Explanada de España promenade and the marina, with the city beach Playa del Postiguet right below the castle.
Alicante's long golden-sand beach a few kilometers north, backed by resorts, apartments, and beach bars; the summer holiday hub, reached easily by TRAM.

A quiet, grid-planned residential barrio southwest of the centre, laid out in the 1880s and still full of low, tiled houses and neighbourhood tapas bars. Casa Mediterráneo, in the restored Benalúa railway station, stands on its edge, with the port and Avenida de Elche a short walk away.
lodging: Hotel Alicante Gran Sol, Affiliated by Meliá
INNSiDE by Meliá Alicante Porta Maris

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though many locals prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: TRAM lines run from around 6am to about 11pm (the L1 line toward Benidorm has limited late service); a few night buses run on summer weekends.
transit.pay: The TRAM and TAM city buses use the rechargeable Móbilis card sold at machines and kiosks; a single city ride is about €1.45 (about US$1.60), cheaper with the card. The TRAM also links Alicante up the coast to El Campello, Benidorm, and Dénia.

transit.m: Bus C-6 to the city center (Renfe station, Luceros), ~25-35 min

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving small change to ~5-10% for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Arroz a banda
food.desc: Rice cooked flat in a wide pan with a deep fish-and-shellfish stock, the fish served separately; the classic Alicante port dish.

places.name: Nou Manolin
places.note: City benchmark for Alicante rice, with a famous standing tapas bar downstairs.

places.name: Darsena
places.note: Marina-side rice specialist with over 100 arroces on the menu.

places.name: Taberna del Raco del Pla
places.note: Long-standing local taberna rated for rice and Alicante market cooking.

food.name: Arroz del senyoret
food.desc: The lazy gentleman's rice: everything peeled and boned before cooking so you never lift a shell, built on the same intense fish stock.

places.name: Darsena
places.note: Harbour institution where rice is the whole point; book for lunch.

places.name: Piripi
places.note: Sister house to Nou Manolin, same kitchen standards and superb tapas bar.

places.name: L'Arruzz Alicante
places.note: Rice-focused modern kitchen; unglamorous branding, excellent arroces.

food.name: Coca amb tonyina
food.desc: Flat enclosed pastry filled with tuna, pine nuts, onion and roasted pepper; the Alicante bakery staple eaten cold at any hour.

places.name: Mercado Central de Alicante
places.note: Modernist market hall; bakery and traiteur stalls sell it by the slice.

places.name: Old-town hornos
places.note: Neighbourhood wood-fired bakeries around the old quarter make it daily.

places.name: Taberna del Raco del Pla
places.note: Serves it as a starter alongside other Alicante market specialities.

food.name: Pericana
food.desc: Mountain dish of dried salted cod or capellan shredded with roasted dried peppers, garlic and lots of olive oil, eaten on bread.

places.name: Nou Manolin
places.note: Tapas bar keeps the inland classics alongside the seafood repertoire.

places.name: Taberna del Raco del Pla
places.note: Traditional taberna that still cooks the Alicante hinterland dishes.

places.name: Cesar Anca
places.note: Creative tapas kitchen that reworks pericana and other regional staples.

food.name: Caldero alicantino
food.desc: Fisherman's two-part meal: rock fish simmered with dried nora peppers, then rice cooked in the broth and served with garlic alioli.

places.name: Darsena
places.note: Does the full caldero properly, with alioli served on the side.

places.name: Nou Manolin
places.note: Classic seafood-stock cooking; ask what the market brought in that day.

places.name: Playa San Juan beach restaurants
places.note: Beachfront chiringuitos north of town cook caldero and rice over fire.

food.name: Turron de Jijona
food.desc: Soft ground-almond and honey nougat from Xixona, 25km inland; the hard Alicante version keeps the almonds whole and brittle.

places.name: Turron shops of Xixona
places.note: The producing town has factory shops and a turron museum; a short bus ride.

places.name: Mercado Central de Alicante
places.note: Confectionery stalls sell both Jijona and Alicante styles year-round.

places.name: Cesar Anca
places.note: Turns turron into desserts, including a nutty turron-custard millefeuille.

food.name: Horchata de chufa
food.desc: Chilled tiger-nut milk, sweet and faintly nutty, drunk with fartons or as a granizado on hot Alicante afternoons.

places.name: Horchaterias of the Explanada
places.note: Palm-lined promenade kiosks pour it iced through the summer.

places.name: Mercado Central de Alicante
places.note: Market bars serve fresh horchata alongside morning coffee and coca.

places.name: Heladeria Peret
places.note: Long-running local ice-cream house doing horchata and turron ice cream.

food.name: Fondillon and Alicante wine
food.desc: Fondillon is a rare aged monastrell wine matured at least ten years, once served to European courts; the DO also makes big modern reds.

places.name: Nou Manolin
places.note: Deep Alicante wine list, including older Fondillon bottles by the glass.

places.name: Cesar Anca
places.note: Well-chosen regional list matched to the tapas menu.

places.name: Casco Antiguo wine bars
places.note: Old-quarter bars pour local monastrell by the glass most evenings.

landmarks: Castillo de Santa Barbara
A sprawling medieval fortress atop 166-metre Mount Benacantil, reached by lift through the rock, commanding sweeping views over city, port, and Mediterranean.
Explanada de Espana
Alicante's signature seafront promenade, its undulating mosaic of 6.6 million marble tesserae rippling beneath four rows of stately palms.
Barrio de Santa Cruz
The old town's most photogenic quarter, a tumble of flower-decked whitewashed lanes and tiny crosses climbing Benacantil's lower slopes.
Playa del Postiguet
The city-centre beach curving beneath the castle crag, where golden sand and calm water sit steps from old-town tapas bars.
Basilica de Santa Maria
Alicante's oldest church, a Gothic basilica raised over the main mosque after the Reconquista, crowned by an exuberant baroque portal.
Concatedral de San Nicolas
The city's serene 17th-century co-cathedral, its sober Herrerian facade concealing a luminous blue-domed interior and lovely cloister.
MARQ (Archaeological Museum of Alicante)
A European Museum of the Year winner presenting Iberian, Roman, and medieval treasures through dazzlingly theatrical galleries.
Mercado Central
A modernist 1920s market hall where locals haggle over glistening seafood, jamon, turron, and produce beneath elegant domed ceilings.
Isla de Tabarca
Spain's smallest inhabited island, a short boat trip away, pairing a walled pirate-era village with pristine marine-reserve snorkelling.
Museo de Arte Contemporaneo (MACA)
Housed in Alicante's oldest baroque building, this free museum displays Eusebio Sempere's collection alongside works by Picasso, Dali, and Miro.

train.note: No international trains. AVE high-speed services from Alicante Terminal reach Madrid in about 2h20, with Euromed and other long-distance trains up the coast to Valencia and Barcelona; for France change at Barcelona Sants. The narrow-gauge TRAM line runs north along the Costa Blanca to Benidorm and Dénia. Renfe booking opens around 60 days out.

bus.note: The Estación de Autobuses is on Calle Sevilla, about 15 minutes' walk from the beach. ALSA runs the domestic network along the coast and to Madrid, Valencia and Murcia; FlixBus and BlaBlaCar Bus cover the European routes. Carry your passport for anything crossing a border.

ferry.note: Alicante is one of only a handful of Spanish ports with a direct crossing to Algeria, though sailings are seasonal, heavily used by the Algerian diaspora in summer and worth booking months ahead. Baleària's Balearic sailings run year-round from the same terminal at the port, a short walk from the Explanada. Check Algerian visa rules well before travelling.

half.name: Altea
half.blurb: Whitewashed hilltop town with a blue-domed church and cobbled streets overlooking the Mediterranean.

half.name: Calpe
half.blurb: Beach town dominated by the dramatic limestone outcrop of Peñón de Ifach jutting into the sea.

half.name: Guadalest
half.blurb: Mountain village built around a clifftop castle ruin, with a turquoise reservoir and nearby waterfalls.

half.name: Murcia
half.blurb: Regional capital with a baroque cathedral and the ornate Casino de Murcia social club, inland from the coast.
